gallery.title: File:Camel Caravan, Axum, Ethiopia (2810054248).jpg
gallery.artist: A. Davey from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest
gallery.description:
I knew I was going to love Axum when I saw this camel caravan out the bus window on the ride in from the airport.  They weren't carrying loads at the time, but I am certain they're working camels heading to or returning from a job.

These are the one-humped camels, or dromedaries, scientific name Camelus dromedarius, which I have to say sounds totally made up.

gallery.title: File:Driving Cattle, Axum, Ethiopia (Detail) (3156437839).jpg
gallery.artist: A. Davey from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest
gallery.description:
Driving cattle near Axum, Ethiopia.  Or are they oxen?  
I guess we'd need to see whether the animals ever do any work.  
Cattle don't work; they don't have to. Suburban cattle often gather with their friends at the club for a round of golf and a luncheon on weekdays.  Others are active in volunteer causes; a few - a very select group - achieve distinction as society hostesses or trophy wives.  Despite their enviable lifestyle, cattle are often depressed and complain of feeling "like just another herd animal with a precarious existence."  That just proves the old adage that the forage is always greener on the other side of the fence.
Oxen are cattle who have broken through the grass ceiling and entered the workforce.* In Ethiopia, that would most often involve pulling carts or plows.  
Unfortunately, oxen are still underrepresented in the professions and executive management, though one dumb ox did manage to get himself elected as the governor of Illinois, while another chewed cud in the Oval Office for eight years under the watchful eye of its herder, an entity whose name on this plane of existence is Dick Cheney.
Getting back to this image, my guess is these are oxen on a break.

*Update:  To the regret of American multinationals seeking to reduce labor costs even further, oxen haven't yet proven suitable for work in call centers or manufacturing facilities, but efforts to achieve a breakthrough are continuing under the auspices of the WTO and World Bank.
categories: Flickr images reviewed by File Upload Bot (Magnus Manske)

gallery.filename: A Pause At Threshing Time, Axum, Ethiopia (3156308439).jpg
gallery.title: File:A Pause At Threshing Time, Axum, Ethiopia (3156308439).jpg
gallery.artist: A. Davey from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest
gallery.description:
The title says it all. Almost.  
The title doesn't tell you to look at the upper right corner of the photograph. There you will find one of the most magnificent trees I "saw" in Ethiopia.  (I've put "saw" in quotes because I didn't notice the tree until I processed this photo today.  This shows once again how easy it is to look without seeing.)
There has been much deforestation in Ethiopia.  Native species have been replaced by Eucalyptus.  I imagine a traveler to Ethiopia in the past (30? 50? 100 years ago?) would have seen more trees like the spreading giant in the upper right.
Note: I took this photo from the other side of the viewing stand at the upper end of the so-called "Queen of Sheba's Palace" on the outskirts of Axum.   
Here's what I was told about the site: it was excavated by a French archaeologist; he never published a report or any findings from his excavation; most, if not all, of the stone walls visible at the site today are reconstructions; there are doubts about the accuracy of the reconstruction.   Oops.

For these reasons, I took only one photograph the "Queen of Sheba's Palace" site, and I chose not to post it.  Fortunately, the area surrounding the site offered interesting scenes such as the one above.

gallery.filename: Farmland In Late Afternoon, Axum, Ethiopia (3160475242).jpg
gallery.title: File:Farmland In Late Afternoon, Axum, Ethiopia (3160475242).jpg
gallery.artist: A. Davey from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest
gallery.description:
The fence in this photo surrounds one of the many stelae fields in the vicinity of Axum.  
I wasn't able to get a good photo of the stelae themselves, but on the whole they were shorter and cruder than the magnificent obelisks shown earlier in my photos of Axum.

I get the impression there used to be many more stelae in and near Axum.

hero.title: File:Stelae Field in Axum, Ethiopia (2830293765).jpg
hero.artist: A. Davey from Where I Live Now: Pacific Northwest
hero.credit:
Stelae Field in Axum, Ethiopia

Uploaded by Elitre
hero.description:
This stelae field is near the so-called Bath of the Queen of Sheba in the Ethiopian city of Axum.
If this site is like the North Stelae Field, where the largest stelae are located, the ground is honeycombed with passages and burial chambers.

These stelae, or obelisks, may be over 1,700 years old.
